title: The Wrong Room
premise: Folklorist Ansel Winterbourne arrives in the isolated village of Hollowmere to record its dying songs, only to find every photograph from his late grandmother's house now shows an extra chair at the table — a chair that wasn't there before. The villagers' songs, sung twice, are invitations: each verse performed a second time lets something older than the village step closer to the hearth. Ansel discovers he is the last blood-descendant of the family that first invited the thing inside generations ago, and that the village has been keeping it fed with borrowed memories and missing neighbors. To survive until sunrise and sever the invitation forever, Ansel must sing the songs himself — once, wrongly, on purpose — accepting the found family of Hollowmere as his own even as the entity wears the faces of everyone he has come to trust.
about_author: Felix Eastwick is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing oral histories in remote coastal villages before turning to horror. He writes in longhand by lamplight and claims he has never once needed to count his doors.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Back
chapters.summary: Ansel arrives in Hollowmere to record folk songs for an archive, renting his late grandmother's cottage. He notices the house feels attentive — doors he counts are sometimes one more in the morning. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: uneasy curiosity masked as professional detachment.

chapters.title: Songs Sung Once
chapters.summary: At the village pub, Ansel coaxes old Tam Yarrow into singing a harvest ballad. When asked for a second verse, Tam goes pale and refuses, and the room empties around him. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: first crack in the village's polite facade; the rule is real.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Sorting his grandmother's photographs, Ansel finds that in every image — across decades — there is now an empty chair at the kitchen table that appears in none of his memory or the negatives' shadows. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: dread arriving through something domestic and small.

chapters.title: Mrs. Pell's Kindness
chapters.summary: Neighbor Mrs. Pell brings bread and warnings wrapped in pleasantries: keep the lights on, count the doors, never answer a knock after the second bell. She calls him 'love' like she's known him always. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: warmth laced with fear — the first thread of belonging.

chapters.title: What the Archive Wouldn't Keep
chapters.summary: In the parish records office, Ansel finds pages torn from the register, all dating to winters when villagers vanished. A librarian whispers that his grandmother didn't leave Hollowmere — she was sent away to break a line. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the past is not past; he was placed here deliberately.

chapters.title: The Second Bell
chapters.summary: Past midnight, a knock comes. Then a second. Ansel keeps the lights burning and counts doors aloud until dawn, hearing patient breathing that matches his own. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: terror of being known, watched, waited for.

chapters.title: Tam's Last Verse
chapters.summary: Tam Yarrow is found at his hearth, smiling, having sung his ballad through twice. His family remembers him fondly but cannot recall his face. POV: Ansel, investigating. Emotional beat: grief and guilt — curiosity has a body count.

chapters.title: The Choir That Isn't
chapters.summary: Ansel records ambient sound at the churchyard and captures voices harmonizing beneath the wind — voices matching the missing. Playing it back summons a figure standing at the gate. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: his own tools turned against him.

chapters.title: Blood in the Register
chapters.summary: Mrs. Pell finally tells him plainly: the Winterbournes made the first invitation two centuries ago, and only their blood can unmake it. Every generation, one is called back. His grandmother fled; the chair waited anyway. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: betrayal by ancestry; he never had the option of invisibility.

chapters.title: Doors That Weren't There Yesterday
chapters.summary: The cottage grows new doorways overnight — doors to rooms Ansel knows aren't real, each warm and lit and furnished with his childhood. The photographs now show the chair occupied by a silhouette. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the entity stops waiting and starts courting.

chapters.title: The Village That Forgot Itself
chapters.summary: Ansel walks Hollowmere and finds residents unable to name their own children, their memories traded away to keep the thing sated. Only those who've shown him kindness retain themselves. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: horror of a community paying rent in identity.

chapters.title: A Meal for Three
chapters.summary: Mrs. Pell sets a table for three and asks Ansel to sit, explaining the ritual of hospitality: what shares your bread may share your name. He eats, and for one evening feels he belongs somewhere. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: found family offered at the worst possible price.

chapters.title: The Face at the Window
chapters.summary: The entity appears wearing his grandmother's face, singing her lullaby through the glass — the song she refused ever to finish. Ansel nearly opens the window; the lights gutter. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: longing weaponized; grief as an unlocked door.

chapters.title: What Grandma Buried
chapters.summary: Digging beneath the hearthstone, Ansel finds his grandmother's journal and a cold iron key: instructions for the Unmaking Song, which must be sung wrong on purpose, alone, by Winterbourne blood, before sunrise on the longest night. Tonight. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: desperate hope with a deadline.

chapters.title: They Take the Kind Ones First
chapters.summary: Mrs. Pell is gone — her cottage empty, her name already fading from the village's mouths. Ansel realizes his presence accelerated the hunger. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: rage and self-blame; the cost of staying invisible too long.

chapters.title: The Longest Night Begins
chapters.summary: Sunset on the solstice. Ansel bars the doors, counts them, lights every lamp, and begins memorizing the Unmaking Song. The house fills with footsteps that politely do not enter. Yet. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: grim resolve; the siege starts.

chapters.title: Every Voice He Ever Recorded
chapters.summary: The entity plays back every voice Ansel archived — Tam, the choir, his grandmother — begging him to stop, to rest, to come sit in the chair. The new doors open one by one. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: his life's work corrupted into a lure.

chapters.title: The Chair Is Warm
chapters.summary: Ansel wakes at the kitchen table he doesn't remember sitting down at, the extra chair beside him still warm, dawn hours away. He understands: part of him has already said yes. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the horror of complicity; the enemy is his own loneliness.

chapters.title: Sung Wrong, On Purpose
chapters.summary: Climax. In the circle of lamplight, Ansel sings the Unmaking Song — flat, broken, deliberately false — naming the thing invited, naming himself its blood, refusing it a home. The house screams through every door at once. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: defiant love as a weapon; belonging claimed, not begged for.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: The entity unravels into the photographs, the chair emptying frame by frame across a century of images. The false doors seal into wallpaper. Ansel survives, hollowed, as grey light fills the kitchen. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: exhausted, uncertain victory.

chapters.title: The Names We Keep Saying
chapters.summary: Ansel spends weeks helping the village remember itself, speaking the missing names aloud daily — Tam, Mrs. Pell, the children — restoring them word by word. Some return; some remain only names. He stays. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: mourning braided with commitment; found family built deliberately.

chapters.title: One Verse, Never Twice
chapters.summary: Epilogue. At the rebuilt hearth, Ansel teaches the village children the old songs with the iron rule attached, and hangs his grandmother's finished portrait — no extra chair. He counts the doors out of habit, then smiles, because they're all his. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: peace earned; belonging chosen at last.
